title: Seedfall
subtitle: Two ends of a cliff city, one soil survey, and the first snow on the way.
story:
You and your partner tend rooftop orchards for the gardeners' guild of a city built five levels up a sea cliff. The first snow is coming. Before it does, every garden's soil must be certified, and the harbor lantern and the lighthouse lamp must be lit to tell the city its gardens are ready for winter.

Player one starts in the harbor garden, at the foot of the cliff; player two starts at the lighthouse, at the city's far end. Certify the soil on your way to the middle garden, then walk home through the far gardens, finishing the full survey on the way. You each test the same survey a different way, so compare answers with your partner. Then light your end of the city.

debrief.title: How the soil survey worked
debrief.intro: You and your partner answered the same four questions about the same soil survey. At every step one of you compared means (t-tests, ANOVA) while the other compared ranks (Wilcoxon and Kruskal-Wallis tests), and you swapped methods along the way. Mostly the two methods agreed. Once, on skewed data, they pointed in opposite directions, and each was right about the question it asks.

ladderPlain.text: In the first puzzle you and your partner compared soil moisture between two gardens, one of you with a t-test on the means and the other with a Wilcoxon rank-sum test on the ranks, and both found Clelia significantly wetter than Ines, because symmetric data give the mean and the median the same story.

In the second puzzle you swapped tests on nitrate in Bice and Zita and both results were significant in opposite directions, the t-test finding Zita higher on average and the Wilcoxon test finding Bice higher in a typical bed, because a few very high Zita readings pull its mean up but count only as a few high ranks.

In the third puzzle you compared pH across the four soil mixes with an overall test followed by a pairwise follow-up (ANOVA then Tukey for one of you, Kruskal-Wallis then Dunn for the other), and both found leaf_mould alone more acidic than the other three.

In the last puzzle you compared phosphorus between all fifteen pairs of gardens and applied the Holm correction, which removes the two pairs (Gemma-Ines and Dora-Zita) that cross p < 0.05 only about as often as fifteen tests would by chance, leaving both methods agreeing on two groups of three gardens.

escapeBrief: Every terrace of the city grows one variety, and every cliff level has its own emblem carved above its gate locks: level 1, the anchor, pistachio with red leaves; level 2, the scallop shell, almond with orange leaves; level 3, the sheaf of wheat, walnut with yellow leaves; level 4, the bell, purple beech with purple leaves; level 5, the five-pointed star, stone pine with green needles. The gate locks made you read each garden's leaf color as you passed. Neither of you saw the whole cliff: the harbor player walked levels 1 to 3 and the lighthouse player levels 3 to 5, so each of you knew three of the five pairs, with the middle garden in common. The planting board asked for all five, one leaf color per emblem, among eight colors, three of which grow nowhere in the city, so the last two could not be guessed. Telling each other what you had seen is what set the seeds. With the board set and the full survey finished, the stair opened to your end's light, and the lever lit it.

An AERIAL photograph of one long, narrow old ITALIAN city strung along a steep rocky SHORELINE like old Genoa stretched out along the coast: a single continuous face of tall, narrow, many-storeyed palazzi in faded ochre, salmon and slate-grey stucco with green shutters, stacked up a near-vertical sea cliff that rises sheer from the water, running for a long way along the shore. A photograph of a real place - NOT a map, NOT a diagram, no labels or borders.

FIVE LEVELS FACING THE WATER: the city climbs the cliff in FIVE clear, stacked levels, stacked almost directly one above another like a tall Genoese palazzo wall, each a long continuous terrace running the whole length of the shore. Every level carries rooftop and terrace GARDENS of nut trees with vividly coloured foliage (gold, russet-red, spring-green, silvery grey-green), and arcaded loggias and balconies that look straight out over the water. Gardens are as prominent as buildings.

THE WAY UP AND DOWN: many tall, slender iron-and-glass LIFT TOWERS with small lit lift houses on top climb between the levels, each joined to a garden by a short iron footbridge at both ends; steep narrow stone stairways zigzag between some neighbouring levels.

ALONG THE TOP: on the clifftop above the highest level, a line of slender old stone bell towers and a narrow stone-lidded aqueduct on low arches run along the length of the city, carrying water to the gardens below.

At the water's edge: a narrow quay and small harbour at one end of the city, a lighthouse on a low rocky point at the other.

PHOTOREALISTIC: a real aerial photograph, natural colour, true-to-life weathered stucco, stone and foliage, realistic scale, restrained light with deep natural shadows, NOT an illustration, NOT a fantasy painting, no glow or bloom, not oversaturated. Very high detail. No people, no lettering, no text, no signs.

VIEW: from the air out over the sea near the harbour end, an oblique view along the whole length of the shoreline city to the lighthouse on its rocky point at the far end, all five levels reading as long stacked terraces of gardens, arcaded loggias and balconies above the water, the tall lift towers rising between them, the bell towers and aqueduct along the clifftop skyline, mountains beyond.

A clear, cold late-autumn evening at blue hour: deep cobalt sky, a rose band low over the sea, warm lamps in the loggias, lift houses and stairway lamps.
